Here is the OpenSCAD script for your Y-junction. I have parameterized the dimensions at the top of the code, making it incredibly easy to tweak the lengths or adjust the angles if you need to fine-tune the fit for your specific tubes.

The OpenSCAD Script

Copy and paste this entire block into a new OpenSCAD file:

// Parametric Y-Junction 
// All measurements are in millimeters (mm)

// --- Parameters ---
$fn = 100; // Resolution/smoothness of the cylinders

// Bottom Stem Dimensions
bottom_od = 6.0;
bottom_id = 3.5;
bottom_stem_length = 15;

// Top Branches Dimensions (Left & Right)
top_od = 9.5;
top_id = 5.5;
top_branch_length = 20;

// Angle of the Y branches from the vertical center axis
branch_angle = 35; 

// --- Geometry Module ---
module y_junction() {
    difference() {
        // 1. OUTER SHELL (The solid body to print)
        union() {
            // Bottom Stem
            cylinder(h=bottom_stem_length, d=bottom_od, center=false);
            
            // Central joint sphere (smooths the exterior intersection)
            translate([0, 0, bottom_stem_length])
                sphere(d=max(bottom_od, top_od));
            
            // Left Branch
            translate([0, 0, bottom_stem_length])
                rotate([0, branch_angle, 0])
                cylinder(h=top_branch_length, d=top_od, center=false);
                
            // Right Branch
            translate([0, 0, bottom_stem_length])
                rotate([0, -branch_angle, 0])
                cylinder(h=top_branch_length, d=top_od, center=false);
        }
        
        // 2. INNER BORE (Subtracting the hollow channels)
        union() {
            // Bottom Stem Hollow (extended down slightly for a clean geometric cut)
            translate([0, 0, -1])
                cylinder(h=bottom_stem_length + 2, d=bottom_id, center=false);
            
            // Central joint hollow sphere (connects the inner channels)
            translate([0, 0, bottom_stem_length])
                sphere(d=max(bottom_id, top_id));
            
            // Left Branch Hollow (extended up for a clean cut)
            translate([0, 0, bottom_stem_length])
                rotate([0, branch_angle, 0])
                cylinder(h=top_branch_length + 2, d=top_id, center=false);
                
            // Right Branch Hollow
            translate([0, 0, bottom_stem_length])
                rotate([0, -branch_angle, 0])
                cylinder(h=top_branch_length + 2, d=top_id, center=false);
        }
    }
}

// Render the final part
y_junction();

How to use this:

turns.prompt_text: How do I install OpenSCAD on my Mac and use it from the terminal?
turns.response_html:
Installing OpenSCAD and driving it from the command line is a great workflow, especially if you want to automate your rendering processes later on.

Here is how to get it installed and configured on your Mac.

1. Installation

The fastest way to install OpenSCAD on macOS is via Homebrew. If you have Homebrew installed, just open your terminal and run:

brew install --cask openscad

(Alternatively, you can download the standard Mac DMG installer directly from the OpenSCAD website and drag it into your Applications folder).

2. Setting up Terminal Access

By default, macOS hides the executable inside the application bundle. To use OpenSCAD as a simple command, you need to tell your terminal where to find it.

Since you are running Fish shell, you can easily create an alias for it. Open your Fish configuration file (usually located at ~/.config/fish/config.fish) and add this line:

alias openscad="/Applications/OpenSCAD.app/Contents/MacOS/OpenSCAD"

Save the file and either restart your terminal or source the config by running source ~/.config/fish/config.fish.

3. Rendering from the Command Line

Now that the CLI is linked, you can compile and render .scad files directly into .stl files without ever opening the graphical interface.

If you saved the Y-junction script I provided earlier as y_junction.scad, you can generate the printable STL by running this command:

openscad -o y_junction.stl y_junction.scad

Helpful CLI Flags:

  • -o [filename]: Specifies the output file. OpenSCAD automatically detects the format you want (STL, 3MF, OBJ) based on the file extension you provide.
  • -D 'var=value': This is incredibly powerful. It allows you to override the variables inside your script directly from the command line.

For example, if you wanted to generate a second Y-junction with a wider 45-degree angle without touching the code, you could run:

openscad -o y_junction_wide.stl -D 'branch_angle=45' y_junction.scad

// Asymmetric Y-Junction (Wye Fitting)
// All measurements are in millimeters (mm)

$fn = 100; // Resolution

// 1. Input Stem (Bottom)
in_od = 9.5;
in_id = 5.5;
in_length = 15;

// 2. Large Output Wing (Top)
out_large_od = 9.5;
out_large_id = 5.5;
out_large_length = 20;

out_small_length = 20;

        union() {
            // Input Stem
            cylinder(h=in_length, d=in_od, center=false);
            
            // Central joint sphere (uses the largest OD to ensure overlap)
            translate([0, 0, in_length])

                cylinder(h=out_large_length, d=out_large_od, center=false);

Stringing on a Y-junction is a rite of passage, especially when dealing with the split paths of the "Y" shape. When the nozzle finishes one branch and travels across the open air to print the other, residual pressure in the nozzle causes the plastic to ooze out, leaving behind a web of strings.

This is especially notorious with both of your materials: TPU is basically liquid rubber that refuses to stop flowing, and PETG HF gets extremely stringy if it has absorbed even a tiny bit of moisture.

Here is how to defeat the stringing in Bambu Studio, ranging from a quick slicer setting to a post-processing trick.

1. The Magic Slicer Setting: "Avoid Crossing Walls"

This is the single best setting for a Y-junction. Instead of taking a straight-line shortcut across the empty air between the two branches, this forces the nozzle to travel inside the perimeter of the printed walls. Any ooze gets deposited safely inside the infill or along the inner wall.

  • In Bambu Studio: Go to Quality -> scroll down to Advanced -> Check the box for Avoid crossing walls.

2. Tweak the Retraction Settings

When the printer jumps across a gap, it pulls the filament back (retraction) to relieve pressure.

  • If you are using TPU: TPU is stretchy. If you retract too much, it acts like a rubber band and jams the extruder. Keep retraction distance low (around 1.0mm to 1.5mm), but try increasing the retraction speed to 30 mm/s to snap the filament back faster.
  • If you are using PETG HF: Stringing usually means the nozzle is slightly too hot, or the filament is wet. Try dropping the nozzle temperature by 5°C.

3. Disable Z-Hop (Z-Lift)

By default, Bambu Studio lifts the print head slightly before moving across a gap so it doesn't scrape the print. With stringy materials, this upward pull acts exactly like pulling a cheese stick apart—it stretches a long, thin string.

  • In Bambu Studio: Go to Printer Settings (the little edit icon next to your printer name) -> Extruder -> Change Z hop when retracting to 0 mm (or select "Normal" instead of "Spiral").

4. The Quick Fix (Don't throw the part away!)

If the junction printed structurally well and the only issue is the stringing in the middle, you don't need to reprint it.

  • Take a lighter, a small torch, or a heat gun, and quickly pass the flame over the strings. They will instantly shrivel up and vanish. Just be quick so you don't warp the main body!

turns.prompt_text: PETG HF

Ah, PETG HF. That explains a lot.

PETG is already notorious for stringing, but the "HF" (High Flow) modifier makes it a completely different beast. To allow the filament to print at those blistering Bambu speeds, manufacturers add compounds that significantly lower the plastic's melt viscosity.

When your A1 is blasting along a straight line, that high-flow liquid state is perfect. But when the nozzle stops extruding to jump across the gap of your Y-junction, that thin, watery plastic just keeps dripping out of the nozzle due to gravity and residual pressure.

Many folks who run print farms or build custom hardware quickly develop a natural intuition for this: if PETG HF is stringing like crazy, you are fighting a pressure problem. Here is exactly how to attack it, starting with the most likely culprit:

1. The "Micro-Pressure Cooker" (Moisture)

PETG is highly hygroscopic—it drinks humidity out of the air. Even if it came vacuum-sealed straight out of the box, it can be wet. As wet filament hits the 250°C nozzle, the microscopic water droplets instantly flash-boil into steam. That steam expands, creating back-pressure that pushes the liquid plastic out of the nozzle during travel moves, creating terrible strings.

  • The Fix: If you hear tiny popping or crackling sounds while it prints, or if the surface looks slightly frosty instead of glossy, it's wet. Dry the spool at 65°C for 8 hours. If you don't have a dedicated dryer, your printer's heated bed and a cardboard box can do the trick.

2. Tame the "High Flow" Melt (Temperature)

If the filament is bone-dry and still stringing, the nozzle is simply too hot for the geometry of a small Y-junction. The default Bambu PETG HF profile is tuned for large, fast models, not small, detailed pipe fittings where the print head has to slow down.

  • The Fix: In Bambu Studio, go to your Filament settings and drop the Nozzle Temperature by 5°C to 10°C (e.g., bring it down from 255°C to 245°C). This thickens the plastic just enough to stop the oozing without sacrificing layer adhesion.

3. The Slicer "Wipe" Setting

When you squeeze a tube of toothpaste and want it to stop, you naturally wipe the nozzle against the toothbrush bristles to break the string. Your printer can do the exact same thing.

  • The Fix: In Bambu Studio, go to the Extruder tab in your Printer settings. Ensure Wipe while retracting is checked. This forces the nozzle to physically wipe itself against the inner wall of the tube before jumping across the gap, cutting the string before it forms.

4. Travel Speed

The less time the nozzle spends traveling in the open air, the less time it has to ooze.

  • The Fix: In the Speed tab, check your Travel speed. For an A1, it should be high—around 500 mm/s to 700 mm/s. If it's moving sluggishly across the gap, bump that travel speed up so it snaps over to the other branch instantly.

turns.prompt_text: Can we lay the y-junction on its side to print it?
turns.response_html:
You absolutely can, and for functional parts that need to handle physical stress or pressure, laying it flat is actually the preferred method among engineers and hardware makers.

That instinct to reorient the model is spot-on. Here is a breakdown of why this works, how it changes the physics of your part, and the minor trade-offs you will have to manage.

The Big Advantage: Structural Strength

When you print a tube standing straight up, the printer builds it like a stack of coins. If you bend the tube, it is very easy to snap it right along one of those horizontal layer lines.

When you lay the Y-junction flat on its side, the printer lays down long, continuous strands of PETG HF from the base of the stem all the way to the tips of the branches. This makes the fitting immensely stronger against snapping or bending because the forces are distributed along the filament strands rather than pulling the layers apart.

As a bonus for your specific stringing issue: printing it flat means the nozzle spends way less time jumping across empty space between the branches, which should naturally reduce the amount of oozing.

The Trade-Offs: Supports and Sagging

Printing a cylinder horizontally introduces two new challenges:

  1. The Underside: The curved bottom of the Y-junction will be printing over thin air, so it requires support material underneath the entire length of the part. The surface finish where the supports touch will be a bit rougher than the smooth top.
  2. The Internal Bore: The inside of the hole will also have to print horizontally. Gravity will try to pull the top of the inner hole down while it prints, which can cause the perfectly round 3.5mm and 5.5mm internal channels to sag and become slightly oval-shaped.

How to set it up in Bambu Studio:

  1. Lay it Flat: Select the Y-junction on the build plate and press the F key on your keyboard (or click the "Lay on Face" icon at the top). Click the flat side of the Y-junction so it drops perfectly flush against the bed.
  2. Support Settings: Go to the Support tab.
    • Enable supports.
    • Set Type to Tree (Auto) or Normal (Snug). Snug supports often peel away from horizontal cylinders very cleanly.
    • Crucial: Make sure Support critical regions only is checked, or uncheck "Support internal structures." You do not want the printer trying to stuff support material inside those tiny 3.5mm internal fluid channels!

Since laying it flat might cause the internal holes to sag slightly, would you like me to show you a classic 3D printing CAD trick where we change the internal hole to a "teardrop" shape to completely eliminate the sagging?

turns.prompt_text: Let's apply this function to the entire scad
turns.response_html:
This is where the magic of code-based CAD really shines. Because OpenSCAD uses modular math, we can completely re-engineer the physics of the entire junction without having to manually redraw a single line.

I have rewritten the script so the entire Y-junction generates completely flat on the virtual floor (the X/Y plane).

Here is exactly what this new code does:

  1. The Teardrop Bore: It replaces every internal cylinder with our new horizontal_teardrop_bore. It calculates the exact 45-degree tangents required so your Bambu printer never has to bridge flat internal overhangs.
  2. The Z-Axis Lock: No matter what angle the branches split off at, the math ensures the point of the teardrop always points straight up towards the sky (+Z axis).
  3. Auto-Bed Leveling: I added a final translation step that automatically lifts the junction by exactly half of its largest diameter. This means when you run your terminal command, it will drop into Bambu Studio resting perfectly flush against the build plate.

The Horizontal Teardrop Y-Junction

Copy this block and run your view_scad_clipboard command to see the new layout, or use your slice_scad_clipboard command to throw it right onto the Bambu bed!

// Insert-Style Barbed Asymmetric Y-Junction 
// Optimized for Horizontal Printing with Teardrop Bores
// All measurements are in millimeters (mm)

$fn = 100; // Resolution for smooth circles

// 1. Input Stem
in_od = 5.5;  
in_id = 3.0;  
in_length = 15;

// 2. Large Output Wing 
out_large_od = 5.5;
out_large_id = 3.0;
out_large_length = 15;
out_large_angle = 20; 

// 3. Small Output Wing 
out_small_od = 3.5; 
out_small_id = 1.5; 
out_small_length = 12;
out_small_angle = -35; 

// Barb (Rib) Settings
barbs_per_arm = 3;
barb_length = 3.0; 
barb_drop = 0.8;   

// --- Geometry Modules ---

module horizontal_barbed_arm(h, od) {
    // Lays the arm flat along the +Y axis
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) { 
        base_h = h - (barbs_per_arm * barb_length); 
        union() {
            cylinder(h=max(0, base_h), d=od);
            for (i = [0 : barbs_per_arm - 1]) {
                translate([0, 0, max(0, base_h) + i * barb_length])
                    cylinder(h=barb_length, d1=od, d2=od - barb_drop);
            }
        }
    }
}

module horizontal_teardrop_bore(h, d) {
    r = d/2;
    // Extrudes along the +Y axis, with the teardrop peak pointing perfectly UP (+Z)
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) 
    linear_extrude(height=h)
    hull() {
        circle(r=r);
        // Extends the peak to an exact 45-degree self-supporting overhang (r * sqrt(2))
        translate([0, r * 1.4142]) square([0.001, 0.001], center=true);
    }
}

module flat_insert_y_junction() {
    // Lift the whole assembly so it rests perfectly on the Bambu build plate
    translate([0, 0, max(in_od, out_large_od, out_small_od)/2])
    difference() {
        // --- OUTER SHELL ---
        union() {
            sphere(d=max(in_od, out_large_od, out_small_od));
            
            // Input Stem (Points straight down)
            rotate([0, 0, 180])
                horizontal_barbed_arm(h=in_length, od=in_od);
            
            // Large Output Wing (Points up and right)
            rotate([0, 0, out_large_angle]) 
                horizontal_barbed_arm(h=out_large_length, od=out_large_od);
                
            // Small Output Wing (Points up and left)
            rotate([0, 0, out_small_angle]) 
                horizontal_barbed_arm(h=out_small_length, od=out_small_od);
        }
        
        // --- INNER BORE ---
        union() {
            // A central sphere bridging the inner fluid channels
            sphere(d=max(in_id, out_large_id, out_small_id));
            
            rotate([0, 0, 180])
                horizontal_teardrop_bore(h=in_length + 2, d=in_id);
            
            rotate([0, 0, out_large_angle])
                horizontal_teardrop_bore(h=out_large_length + 2, d=out_large_id);
                
            rotate([0, 0, out_small_angle])
                horizontal_teardrop_bore(h=out_small_length + 2, d=out_small_id);
        }
    }
}

// Render the final part
flat_insert_y_junction();

When you hit print on this, remember to turn your supports back on in Bambu Studio, but double-check that "Support internal structures" is turned OFF (or check the box for "Support critical regions only"). You don't want the slicer trying to jam support trees inside those beautiful self-supporting teardrop channels!

Would you like me to walk you through adjusting the infill settings for this horizontal layout to ensure the junction holds up against the internal fluid pressure?

turns.prompt_text: Yes please
turns.response_html:
When it comes to holding fluid or air pressure, the 3D printing community has a golden rule: Infill doesn't hold water, walls do. Because FDM printing lays down plastic in microscopic rows, gaps between those rows are the enemy of a pressurized system. While infill provides structural rigidity against crushing forces, it is the outer and inner walls that actually seal the system.

Here is exactly how to set up Bambu Studio so this horizontal Y-junction doesn't weep or leak under pressure:

1. Maximize Wall Loops (Perimeters)

This is the single most important setting for creating a watertight part.

  • The Setting: Go to the Strength tab and change Wall loops to 4 or 5.
  • The Physics: By forcing the printer to draw 4 solid outlines before it even thinks about infill, you are creating a thick, solid shell. Because your smallest branch only has an outer diameter of 3.5mm and an inner diameter of 1.5mm, setting this to 4 walls means the slicer will actually make that tiny branch 100% solid plastic.

2. Choose the Right Infill Pattern

Never use the default "Grid" infill for PETG HF, especially for parts that need to hold pressure. Grid infill crosses over its own lines on the same layer, which causes the nozzle to scrape over existing plastic, creating microscopic gaps and increasing stringing.

  • The Setting: In the Strength tab, change the Sparse infill pattern to Gyroid.
  • The Physics: Gyroid is a continuous, 3D-wavy structure that never crosses itself on a single layer. It distributes physical stress equally in all directions (X, Y, and Z), which perfectly mimics natural organic structures and is ideal for pressurized vessels.

3. Increase Top and Bottom Shells

Because you are printing this cylinder lying on its side, the "Top" and "Bottom" of the print are actually the long exterior sides of your tubes. If these are too thin, fluid will easily seep through the layer lines.

  • The Setting: In the Strength tab, look under Top/bottom shells and change both Top shell layers and Bottom shell layers to 5.

4. Overlap Settings (The Secret Sauce)

To ensure the infill bonds perfectly to the thick walls you just created, you want to force the nozzle to shove a little extra plastic into the corners.

  • The Setting: Still in the Strength tab, scroll down to the Advanced section. Find Infill/wall overlap and bump it from the default 15% up to 25%.

A Quick Preview Check

Before you hit print, always slice the model and use the slider bar on the right side of the screen to scroll down through the layers. Look closely at that tiny 3.5mm branch. With these settings, it shouldn't show any infill at all—it should just be a solid ring of wall lines hugging that teardrop hole.

Would you like to fire this off to the A1 and see how perfectly those teardrops bridge, or do you need to adjust any of the barb lengths before committing to the print?

This is one of those brilliant little engineering tricks that bridges the gap between software design and the physical reality of melting plastic.

Why Horizontal Circles Fail

When your Bambu A1 tries to print a perfect tube laying flat on its side, the bottom and the sides print beautifully. But as the nozzle reaches the very top inner ceiling of the hole, it is forced to extrude plastic perfectly horizontally over empty air. Gravity immediately grabs that hot PETG HF and pulls it down, causing the top of the hole to sag. If your inner hole was perfectly 5.5mm in CAD, it might print as an oval that's only 5.0mm tall, and your fluid flow gets restricted.

The "Teardrop" Solution

Instead of a perfect circle, we change the internal channel to a teardrop shape. The bottom half remains a perfect half-circle for the fluid to flow through smoothly. But the top half tapers up into a 45-degree point, like the roof of a house.

FDM 3D printers are incredibly good at printing 45-degree angles because each new layer overlaps the previous one enough to support itself without sagging.

How to do it in OpenSCAD

Because you are using OpenSCAD, creating this is incredibly elegant. We can write a tiny custom module that uses a hull() command to stretch a circle up to a point.

Here is the exact code block you would add to the top of your script:

module teardrop_cylinder(h, d) {
    r = d/2;
    // We lay it flat along the Y axis, with the point facing UP (Z-axis)
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) 
    linear_extrude(height=h)
    hull() {
        // The perfectly round bottom half
        circle(r=r, $fn=100);
        // The 45-degree self-supporting roof peak
        translate([0, r * sqrt(2)]) square(0.001, center=true);
    }
}

The Catch: Orientation is Everything

For this trick to work, the point of the teardrop must point directly UP toward the sky when it is sitting on your printer's build plate. If the teardrop points sideways, it defeats the entire purpose and will print terribly.

This means we have to design the Y-junction with the assumption that it will be sliced exactly as it is generated, lying flat on the ground.

turns.response_html:
Switching back to the outer sleeve design is a great call, especially if your tubes are somewhat rigid. A sleeve naturally forces the tubes into alignment and gives you a large surface area for friction or adhesives.

However, moving the teardrop trick to a sleeve introduces a fascinating physical catch that we have to engineer our way around.

The Teardrop Leak Dilemma

If we make the entire inner hole a teardrop shape, and you shove a perfectly round 9.5mm tube into it, the bottom and sides will touch perfectly. But at the very top, that 45-degree teardrop "roof" will sit above your round tube, leaving a tiny, triangular gap running the length of the connection. The moment you apply pressure, fluid or air will shoot right out of that gap.

The Solution: We must make the pockets where the tubes actually sit perfectly round so they seal airtight. We will only use the teardrop shape for the deeper central fluid channels where the tubes don't reach.

Because the pockets are round and printing horizontally, the very top ceiling of the 9.5mm opening might sag a tiny fraction of a millimeter. That is actually perfect—it will act as a natural friction clamp when you force the tube inside.

The Flat Outer Sleeve Script

Here is the fully engineered sleeve design. It features thick 2.5mm outer walls to hold pressure, built-in tube stops so you can't push the tubes in too far, and it lays perfectly flat for printing.

Copy this and run your slice_scad_clipboard command to drop it right onto your Bambu build plate!

// Flat Outer Sleeve Y-Junction (Tubes insert INSIDE)
// Optimized for Horizontal Printing

$fn = 100; // Smooth circles

// 1. Input Stem (Fits 9.5mm OD tube)
in_tube_od = 9.5;   // The perfectly round pocket for the tube
in_fluid_id = 5.5;  // The central teardrop flow channel
in_shell_od = 14.5; // Outer plastic shell (2.5mm thick wall)
in_length = 22;     // Total length of this arm
in_pocket_depth = 16; // How far the tube slides in before hitting the stop

// 2. Large Output Wing (Fits 9.5mm OD tube)
out_large_tube_od = 9.5;
out_large_fluid_id = 5.5;
out_large_shell_od = 14.5;
out_large_length = 22;
out_large_pocket_depth = 16;
out_large_angle = 20; 

// 3. Small Output Wing (Fits 6.0mm OD tube)
out_small_tube_od = 6.0;
out_small_fluid_id = 3.5;
out_small_shell_od = 11.0;
out_small_length = 20;
out_small_pocket_depth = 14;
out_small_angle = -35; 

// --- Geometry Modules ---

module horizontal_arm_shell(h, od) {
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) cylinder(h=h, d=od);
}

module horizontal_teardrop_bore(h, d) {
    r = d/2;
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) 
    linear_extrude(height=h)
    hull() {
        circle(r=r);
        // The 45-degree self-supporting roof peak
        translate([0, r * 1.4142]) square([0.001, 0.001], center=true);
    }
}

module horizontal_tube_pocket(total_h, pocket_depth, tube_od, fluid_id) {
    // 1. The perfectly round pocket for the tube to seal against
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) 
        translate([0, 0, total_h - pocket_depth]) 
        cylinder(h=pocket_depth + 0.1, d=tube_od);
        
    // 2. The teardrop fluid channel bridging the center
    horizontal_teardrop_bore(h=total_h, d=fluid_id);
}

module flat_sleeve_y_junction() {
    // Lift the whole assembly so it rests exactly flush on the build plate
    translate([0, 0, max(in_shell_od, out_large_shell_od, out_small_shell_od)/2])
    difference() {
        // --- OUTER SHELL ---
        union() {
            sphere(d=max(in_shell_od, out_large_shell_od, out_small_shell_od));
            
            rotate([0, 0, 180]) 
                horizontal_arm_shell(h=in_length, od=in_shell_od);
                
            rotate([0, 0, out_large_angle]) 
                horizontal_arm_shell(h=out_large_length, od=out_large_shell_od);
                
            rotate([0, 0, out_small_angle]) 
                horizontal_arm_shell(h=out_small_length, od=out_small_shell_od);
        }
        
        // --- INNER BORE (Subtracting the pockets and fluid channels) ---
        union() {
            // Central sphere connecting the fluid channels
            sphere(d=max(in_fluid_id, out_large_fluid_id, out_small_fluid_id));
            
            rotate([0, 0, 180]) 
                horizontal_tube_pocket(total_h=in_length, pocket_depth=in_pocket_depth, tube_od=in_tube_od, fluid_id=in_fluid_id);
                
            rotate([0, 0, out_large_angle]) 
                horizontal_tube_pocket(total_h=out_large_length, pocket_depth=out_large_pocket_depth, tube_od=out_large_tube_od, fluid_id=out_large_fluid_id);
                
            rotate([0, 0, out_small_angle]) 
                horizontal_tube_pocket(total_h=out_small_length, pocket_depth=out_small_pocket_depth, tube_od=out_small_tube_od, fluid_id=out_small_fluid_id);
        }
    }
}

// Render the final part
flat_sleeve_y_junction();

turns.prompt_text: Alright, let's go back over the outer y-junction. Let's make sure it has ribs on the inside of it. And let's make sure it has the teardrop.
turns.response_html:
Combining all three of those elements—an outer sleeve, internal ribs, and the horizontal teardrop bore—is the ultimate test of 3D printing geometry.

I have written the script to do exactly this. However, before you send it to the printer, we need to talk about what happens when melted plastic meets this specific combination of features.

The Physics of Horizontal Internal Ribs

We added the teardrop shape to the central fluid channel because a printer cannot print a perfectly flat ceiling inside a horizontal tube without the plastic sagging.

By adding internal ribs to the horizontal tube pockets, we are slightly reintroducing that problem. The ribs require the printer to step the internal diameter inward by 0.6mm. On the left and right sides of the tube, this prints perfectly. But at the very top ceiling of the pocket, the nozzle has to extrude a tiny 0.3mm shelf of plastic mid-air to form the catch of the rib.

Because the step is so small, your Bambu A1 and the PETG HF will likely power through it, but you might see a few tiny, rough strands of plastic inside the pocket where gravity pulled the rib down slightly. Since your tubes will be sliding in and crushing against these ribs anyway, a little roughness might actually increase the grip!

The Ultimate Ribbed & Teardropped Sleeve Script

Here is the complete OpenSCAD script. It lays flat, features the self-supporting teardrop channels in the center so the fluid flow stays perfectly open, and contains stacked internal barbs inside the perfectly round tube pockets to grab the outside of your tubes.

// Flat Outer Sleeve Y-Junction 
// Features: Internal Ribs & Horizontal Teardrop Bores

$fn = 100; // Smooth circles

// 1. Input Stem (Fits 9.5mm OD tube)
in_tube_od = 9.5;   
in_fluid_id = 5.5;  
in_shell_od = 14.5; 
in_length = 22;     
in_pocket_depth = 16; 

// 2. Large Output Wing (Fits 9.5mm OD tube)
out_large_tube_od = 9.5;
out_large_fluid_id = 5.5;
out_large_shell_od = 14.5;
out_large_length = 22;
out_large_pocket_depth = 16;
out_large_angle = 20; 

// 3. Small Output Wing (Fits 6.0mm OD tube)
out_small_tube_od = 6.0;
out_small_fluid_id = 3.5;
out_small_shell_od = 11.0;
out_small_length = 20;
out_small_pocket_depth = 14;
out_small_angle = -35; 

// Internal Barb Settings
barbs_per_arm = 3;
barb_length = 2.5; 
barb_grip_drop = 0.6; // The pinch: drops the diameter to grip the tube

// --- Geometry Modules ---

module horizontal_arm_shell(h, od) {
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) cylinder(h=h, d=od);
}

module horizontal_teardrop_bore(h, d) {
    r = d/2;
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) 
    linear_extrude(height=h)
    hull() {
        circle(r=r);
        // The 45-degree self-supporting roof peak
        translate([0, r * 1.4142]) square([0.001, 0.001], center=true);
    }
}

module horizontal_barbed_pocket(total_h, pocket_depth, tube_od, fluid_id) {
    // 1. Teardrop fluid channel bridging the center
    horizontal_teardrop_bore(h=total_h, d=fluid_id);
    
    // 2. The pocket with internal ribs
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) 
        translate([0, 0, total_h - pocket_depth]) {
            
            base_pocket = pocket_depth - (barbs_per_arm * barb_length);
            
            // Smooth section at the bottom of the pocket (tube stop)
            if (base_pocket > 0) {
                cylinder(h=base_pocket, d=tube_od);
            }
            
            // Stacked internal barbs
            for (i = [0 : barbs_per_arm - 1]) {
                translate([0, 0, max(0, base_pocket) + i * barb_length])
                    // d2 is the wide opening facing the outside
                    // d1 is the narrow pinch facing the inside stop
                    cylinder(h=barb_length + 0.01, d1=tube_od - barb_grip_drop, d2=tube_od);
            }
        }
}

module flat_ribbed_sleeve_y_junction() {
    // Lifts the assembly so it rests perfectly flush on the bed
    translate([0, 0, max(in_shell_od, out_large_shell_od, out_small_shell_od)/2])
    difference() {
        // --- OUTER SHELL ---
        union() {
            sphere(d=max(in_shell_od, out_large_shell_od, out_small_shell_od));
            rotate([0, 0, 180]) horizontal_arm_shell(h=in_length, od=in_shell_od);
            rotate([0, 0, out_large_angle]) horizontal_arm_shell(h=out_large_length, od=out_large_shell_od);
            rotate([0, 0, out_small_angle]) horizontal_arm_shell(h=out_small_length, od=out_small_shell_od);
        }
        
        // --- INNER BORE ---
        union() {
            // Central fluid intersection
            sphere(d=max(in_fluid_id, out_large_fluid_id, out_small_fluid_id));
            
            rotate([0, 0, 180]) horizontal_barbed_pocket(total_h=in_length, pocket_depth=in_pocket_depth, tube_od=in_tube_od, fluid_id=in_fluid_id);
            rotate([0, 0, out_large_angle]) horizontal_barbed_pocket(total_h=out_large_length, pocket_depth=out_large_pocket_depth, tube_od=out_large_tube_od, fluid_id=out_large_fluid_id);
            rotate([0, 0, out_small_angle]) horizontal_barbed_pocket(total_h=out_small_length, pocket_depth=out_small_pocket_depth, tube_od=out_small_tube_od, fluid_id=out_small_fluid_id);

    }

turns.prompt_text: Why is only the inside of the y-junction teardrop shaped?
turns.response_html:
That is an incredibly sharp question. It is exactly the kind of question a mechanical engineer asks when moving a design from a computer screen into physical reality.

It comes down to two very different physical problems: how FDM 3D printers handle external arches vs. internal ceilings, and how physical tubes seal.

Here is why we only apply the teardrop to that deep internal channel:

1. The Outer Shell Builds Like a Dome

When your Bambu A1 prints the outside of a horizontal pipe, it builds it from the ground up like a Roman arch.

  • The bottom half is supported either by the build plate or by the tree supports we turned on.
  • As the printer moves past the equator and starts building the top half, each new layer steps slightly inward. Because it's stepping inward gradually, each layer has plenty of plastic directly underneath it to rest on.
  • By the time it reaches the very top center line, the gap is microscopic, and it closes the pipe perfectly. The outside naturally supports itself, so we get to keep our standard, clean cylindrical look.

2. The Tube Pockets Must Seal

The pockets at the ends of the Y-junction—where your physical tubes actually slide in—must remain perfectly round.

  • If we made those pockets teardrop-shaped, your perfectly round tubes would push in, but that 45-degree triangular peak would sit empty right above the tube.
  • The moment fluid hit that junction, it would bypass the tube entirely and shoot straight out of that triangular gap. We leave these perfectly round so the plastic hugs the tube 360 degrees.

3. The Deep Fluid Channel Has No Support

Deep inside the exact center of the Y-junction, past where your tubes stop, is the central fluid channel.

  • The printer has to build a ceiling over this empty void. Unlike the outside arch, this inner ceiling is concave.
  • If we left it as a perfect circle, the printer would reach the top of the hole and try to extrude a flat line of hot plastic directly across thin air. Gravity would immediately pull it down, creating a saggy mess that restricts your fluid flow.
  • Because we can't easily dig support material out of a tiny 3.5mm or 5.5mm hole, we change it to a teardrop. That creates a 45-degree peaked roof, allowing the plastic layers to overlap and support themselves as they close the gap.

By mixing these geometries, we get the best of all worlds: a smooth external look, perfectly round airtight seals for your tubes, and clean, self-supporting internal plumbing.

Ah, the classic nozzle collision. You fix the stringing, and immediately run into the next boss battle.

What you are experiencing is likely a combination of two things fighting against you: our anti-stringing settings and the physical shape of a cylinder resting on a flat bed.

When we set Z-hop to 0 mm to stop the PETG HF from stringing, we told the printer to drag the nozzle perfectly level across the part during travel moves. If the plastic curls up even a fraction of a millimeter as it cools, that hot nozzle acts like a plow and rams right into it. Combine that with the fact that a cylinder laying flat only touches the bed along a very thin, narrow line, and it is incredibly easy for the nozzle to knock the entire part loose.

Because your Y-junction is a round pipe laying on its side, its actual contact patch with your A1's build plate is tiny.   • Change to: Outer brim only
  • Search for: Brim width

Bambu Lab officially supports TPU 95A (which is firm, like a skateboard wheel). TPU 85A is incredibly soft—it is basically like trying to push a cooked wet noodle through your extruder. Because it is so difficult to print, they leave it up to the community to create custom profiles for it.

How to Build Your Custom 85A Profile

1. Set the Base Profile Go to the Filament section on the left sidebar. Click the dropdown and select Generic TPU.

2. Open the Filament Settings Click that tiny edit icon right next to the filament dropdown (the square with a pen we found earlier). A new window will pop up.

Here is the exact trick to popping that AMS tube out of the print head so you can feed your TPU:

1. Unload the Current Filament

Before disconnecting anything, look at your A1's touchscreen. Go to the Filament menu and select Unload to make sure the hotend is completely empty and the AMS has pulled the current plastic back out of the print head.

2. Locate the 4-in-1 Hub

Look at the very top of the print head (the toolhead moving around on the X-axis). You will see a clear and black plastic adapter where all four tubes from the AMS Lite plug in.

Pick one of the four tubes to remove (it doesn't matter which one).

  • Using your fingernail or a pair of tweezers, press that tiny ring firmly DOWN towards the print head.
  • While holding that ring pushed down, pull the PTFE tube UP.

It should pop out smoothly with almost zero resistance. If it feels like it's fighting you, make sure that little ring is pushed all the way down.

4. Feed the TPU

  1. Take the raw end of your TPU 85A from the external spool. (Make sure the tip is cut at a sharp 45-degree angle so it's pointy).
  2. Shove that pointy end straight down into the empty hole you just created on the hub.
  3. Keep pushing it down until you feel it hit the extruder gears inside (usually an inch or two down).
  4. On your A1's touchscreen, hit the Extrude or Load button so the gears grab the rubber and pull it into the hot nozzle.

Ah, you have encountered the final boss of 3D printing fluid components: the "sweating" print. It is incredibly satisfying that your mechanical fit and barbs worked perfectly, but seeing water bead up directly through solid plastic walls is definitely frustrating!

This happens because FDM 3D prints aren't truly solid. They are thousands of microscopic plastic strings stacked on top of each other. Under pressure, water will find the microscopic valleys between those layer lines and slowly push its way through the walls.

Looking across the broader maker community—from hydroponic farmers building custom drip systems to PC builders doing custom water-cooling loops—there are two main schools of thought for making FDM parts 100% watertight.

Method 1: The Chemical Seal (Fixing the part you just printed)

Since you already have a part that mechanically fits your tubes perfectly, the fastest route is often to just seal the one in your hand rather than reprinting.

  • The Superglue (CA Glue) Wash: If you have ultra-thin, liquid superglue, you can drop it around the outside (or inside) of the junction. Because it is so thin, capillary action sucks it deep into the microscopic layer lines, plugging the microscopic holes instantly as it cures.
  • Two-Part Epoxy/Polyurethane: Painting a thin layer of clear epoxy resin or brushing on a polyurethane clear coat over the outside of the print creates an impenetrable shell.

Method 2: The "Over-Squish" (Reprinting for a watertight seal)

If you would rather tune the printer so the part comes off the bed inherently watertight without needing messy glue, we have to intentionally over-stuff the plastic to force those layer lines to fuse into a single solid mass.

In Bambu Studio, you can make these three quick tweaks to your PETG profile:

  1. Increase Temperature: Bump your nozzle temperature up by 5°C to 10°C. Hotter plastic melts into the layer below it much better, eliminating the micro-gaps.
  2. Increase Flow Ratio: Go to the Filament settings and bump the Flow Ratio up by about 0.05 (e.g., from 0.95 to 1.00). This intentionally over-extrudes plastic, cramming extra material into any empty microscopic voids.
  3. Randomize the Seam: Go to the Quality tab and change the Seam Position to Random. A perfectly straight Z-seam creates a continuous weak point for water to travel down. Randomizing it scatters those start/stop points so water hits dead ends.

turns.prompt_text: I think chemically sealing would be a little easier, but would hot glue work as well?
turns.response_html:
Hot glue is a fantastic tool for a lot of DIY projects, but for sealing a pressurized 3D-printed water fitting, it is actually one of the worst options you could choose.

Here is the physics behind why hot glue will likely fail you here:

1. It Fails the "Wicking" Test

The reason water is leaking through your print is that it is finding microscopic valleys and tunnels between the plastic layer lines. To seal those tunnels, you need a liquid with low viscosity (water-thin) so it can get sucked deep into the plastic via capillary action.

Hot glue is highly viscous (thick and goopy). It will just sit on the very top of the surface like a heavy blanket. It won't penetrate the pores to actually plug the micro-leaks.

2. Poor Surface Adhesion Under Pressure

Hot glue doesn't chemically bond to FDM plastics like PETG or PLA; it just mechanically grips the surface texture. As soon as water pressure builds up inside the tube, that water will find a way to push directly underneath the hot glue layer, eventually peeling it off the plastic entirely.

What You Actually Need

To stop the sweating, you need something that either melts into the plastic or forms a hard, impenetrable chemical shell.

  • Thin Superglue (Cyanoacrylate / CA Glue): This is the holy grail for leaky prints. Because it is as thin as water, it gets sucked right into the layer lines exactly where the water is trying to escape. It cures in seconds and permanently plugs the holes from the inside out.
  • Clear Nail Polish: If you don't have superglue, stealing a bottle of clear nail polish and painting it over the outside of the print works surprisingly well. It is thin enough to fill the gaps and dries into a hard acrylic shell.
  • Plumber's PVC Primer/Cement: If you have this lying around, it actually melts the outer layer of the plastic slightly, fusing all those microscopic gaps shut.

If you take a quick look around your workspace, what kind of glues, epoxies, or clear coats do you currently have on hand? I can tell you exactly which one will give you the best watertight seal.

turns.prompt_text: could nail polish be used in place of paint?
turns.response_html:
Yes, absolutely! In fact, if you ask around the overlapping worlds of miniature painters, custom lure makers, and DIY hardware hackers, nail polish is considered a legendary secret weapon for jobs exactly like this.

Chemically speaking, nail polish isn't just cosmetic; it is a highly durable nitrocellulose lacquer. For sealing a pressurized 3D print, it is actually far superior to standard craft paint.

Here is the breakdown of why it works so beautifully:

1. The Solvent "Bite"

Standard acrylic paints are water-based. They just sit on top of the plastic and can easily flake off or wash away under pressure. Nail polish uses aggressive chemical solvents (like ethyl acetate). When you brush it onto a PETG or PLA print, those solvents actually "bite" into the plastic, slightly melting the surface and physically fusing the microscopic layer lines together.

2. Capillary Action

Because nail polish is relatively thin, it excels at finding tiny gaps. When you brush it horizontally across the layer lines of your printed tube, it will wick deep into those microscopic valleys where the water has been escaping.

3. The Hard Shell Finish

Once the solvent evaporates, the lacquer cures into an incredibly tough, waterproof, and slightly flexible acrylic shell.

How to Apply It for Maximum Sealing:

  • Dry It Out: This is the most critical step. Since your part was already weeping water, you must make sure it is bone dry before painting. If there is moisture trapped in the micro-tunnels, the polish won't stick. (Hitting it with a hairdryer for a couple of minutes works great).
  • The First Coat (The Primer): Brush on a relatively thin layer. Don't worry about it looking pretty yet; just work the bristles into the layer lines so the polish sinks into the grooves.
  • The Second Coat (The Shell): Wait about 15 minutes for the first coat to get tacky, then apply a thicker second coat to create the final waterproof jacket.

Whether you use clear polish or a bright neon color, the chemical sealing properties are exactly the same.

turns.response_html:
Twisting a pipe into a threaded fitting is exactly how heavy-duty garden hoses and commercial plumbing fixtures work, so your engineering instincts are spot on.

However, translating that into FDM 3D printing introduces a massive physical roadblock. If we print internal threads while the Y-junction is laying flat on the bed, the printer has to draw a spiral mid-air across the ceiling of the hole. Gravity will instantly pull those tiny threads down, turning the inside of your pipe fitting into a messy, stringy bird's nest that will completely block your tube from going in at all.

Instead of fighting gravity with horizontal threads, we can solve the root problem—the pipe being too hard to push in—by changing the geometry of the entrance and softening the "bite" of the barbs.

The "Funnel & Glide" Solution

To make inserting the pipe significantly easier without losing the zip-tie locking effect, I have made two major mechanical changes to the script:

  1. The Entrance Funnel (Chamfer): The very outside edge of every opening is now flared out 1.5mm wider than your pipe. When you push the pipe in, you don't have to perfectly align it; the funnel will grab the end of the tube and naturally squeeze it into the center.
  2. Softer Barbs: I cut the "pinch" of the internal barbs in half (dropping from a 0.8mm ledge down to a 0.4mm ledge). It will still lock the pipe in place so it can't back out, but it takes drastically less physical force to push it past the ramps.

Here is the updated script, reverted back to the Y-intersection (with the 20-degree and 35-degree sweeps) and upgraded with the easy-insert funnels:

// Features: Easy-Insert Chamfer & Shallow Locking Barbs

$fn = 100; // Smooth circles

// --- Scale Multipliers ---
global_scale = 1.06; // +6% overall size
small_scale = 1.10;  // +10% for the small branch

// 1. Input Stem
in_tube_od = 9.5 * global_scale;   
in_fluid_id = 5.5 * global_scale;  
in_shell_od = 14.5 * global_scale; 
in_length = 22 * global_scale;     
in_pocket_depth = 16 * global_scale; 

// 2. Large Output Wing

out_large_fluid_id = 5.5 * global_scale;
out_large_shell_od = 14.5 * global_scale;
out_large_length = 22 * global_scale;
out_large_pocket_depth = 16 * global_scale;
out_large_angle = 20; 

// 3. Small Output Wing
out_small_tube_od = 6.0 * small_scale;
out_small_fluid_id = 3.5 * small_scale;
out_small_shell_od = 11.0 * small_scale;
out_small_length = 20 * small_scale;
out_small_pocket_depth = 14 * small_scale;
out_small_angle = -35; 

// Internal Barb Settings 
barbs_per_arm = 4;
barb_length = 2.5; 
barb_grip_drop = 0.4; // Reduced for much easier insertion

// --- Geometry Modules ---

module horizontal_arm_shell(h, od) {
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) cylinder(h=h, d=od);
}

module horizontal_circular_bore(h, d) {
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) cylinder(h=h, d=d);
}

module horizontal_barbed_pocket(total_h, pocket_depth, tube_od, fluid_id) {
    // 1. Perfectly round central fluid channel
    horizontal_circular_bore(h=total_h, d=fluid_id);
    
    // 2. The pocket with funnels and directional barbs
    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) 
        translate([0, 0, total_h - pocket_depth]) {
            // Reserve 2mm at the top for the funnel
            base_pocket = pocket_depth - (barbs_per_arm * barb_length) - 2; 
            
            // Smooth section at the bottom of the pocket (tube stop)
            if (base_pocket > 0) {
                cylinder(h=base_pocket, d=tube_od);
            }
            
            // Directional barbs (Softer 0.4mm ramps)
            for (i = [0 : barbs_per_arm - 1]) {
                translate([0, 0, max(0, base_pocket) + i * barb_length])
                    cylinder(h=barb_length + 0.01, d1=tube_od - barb_grip_drop, d2=tube_od);
            }
            
            // The Entrance Funnel (Chamfer)
            translate([0, 0, max(0, base_pocket) + (barbs_per_arm * barb_length)])
                cylinder(h=2.01, d1=tube_od, d2=tube_od + 1.5);
        }
}

module flat_ribbed_sleeve_y_junction() {
    translate([0, 0, max(in_shell_od, out_large_shell_od, out_small_shell_od)/2])
    difference() {
        // --- OUTER SHELL ---
        union() {
            sphere(d=max(in_shell_od, out_large_shell_od, out_small_shell_od));
            rotate([0, 0, 180]) horizontal_arm_shell(h=in_length, od=in_shell_od);
            rotate([0, 0, out_large_angle]) horizontal_arm_shell(h=out_large_length, od=out_large_shell_od);
            rotate([0, 0, out_small_angle]) horizontal_arm_shell(h=out_small_length, od=out_small_shell_od);
        }
        
        // --- INNER BORE ---
        union() {
            sphere(d=max(in_fluid_id, out_large_fluid_id, out_small_fluid_id));
            rotate([0, 0, 180]) horizontal_barbed_pocket(total_h=in_length, pocket_depth=in_pocket_depth, tube_od=in_tube_od, fluid_id=in_fluid_id);
            rotate([0, 0, out_large_angle]) horizontal_barbed_pocket(total_h=out_large_length, pocket_depth=out_large_pocket_depth, tube_od=out_large_tube_od, fluid_id=out_large_fluid_id);
            rotate([0, 0, out_small_angle]) horizontal_barbed_pocket(total_h=out_small_length, pocket_depth=out_small_pocket_depth, tube_od=out_small_tube_od, fluid_id=out_small_fluid_id);
        }
    }
}

// Render the final part
flat_ribbed_sleeve_y_junction();

The Plumber's Secret Trick

Even with the updated funnel and softer barbs, you are still fighting friction. Before you try to attach the pipes to the next printed version, take the end of your physical tube and dip it into a cup of very hot (or boiling) water for about 10 seconds.

The heat temporarily softens the plastic/rubber of the tube, allowing it to effortlessly glide over the printed barbs. As it cools back down to room temperature, it will shrink-wrap itself around the barbs, creating an incredibly tight, permanent seal.

barb_length = 2.5; 
barb_grip_drop = 0.4;

    rotate([-90, 0, 0]) cylinder(h=h, d=od);
}

module horizontal_circular_bore(h, d) {

}

module horizontal_tapered_pocket(total_h, pocket_depth, tube_od_target, fluid_id) {
    // Calculate the cone diameters based on the target tube OD
    d_top = tube_od_target + (taper_range / 2); // Oversized entrance
    d_bottom = tube_od_target - (taper_range / 2); // Undersized stop
    
    // 1. Perfectly round central fluid channel

    // 2. The conical pocket with funnels and directional barbs

$fn = 100; // Smooth circles

// We are testing the 9.5mm pipe connection (scaled +6% as previously established)
tube_od_target = 9.5 * 1.06; 
fluid_id = 5.5 * 1.06;
pocket_depth = 16 * 1.06;

// Minimal shell to save filament (just enough for structural integrity)
wall_thickness = 2.5;
shell_od = tube_od_target + (wall_thickness * 2);

// Barb standard settings
barbs_per_arm = 4;
barb_length = 2.5; 

// --- The Test Sleeve Generator ---
module test_sleeve(taper_range, barb_grip_drop, label_text) {
    d_top = tube_od_target + (taper_range / 2);
    d_bottom = tube_od_target - (taper_range / 2);
    
    // Calculate space for the smooth stop at the bottom of the pocket
    base_pocket_h = pocket_depth - (barbs_per_arm * barb_length) - 2; 

    difference() {
        // 1. The minimal outer shell
        cylinder(h=pocket_depth, d=shell_od);

        translate([0, 0, -1]) 
            cylinder(h=pocket_depth + 2, d=fluid_id);

            d_at_base_top = d_bottom + (base_pocket_h / pocket_depth) * taper_range;
            
            // Smooth tapered stop
            if (base_pocket_h > 0) {
                translate([0, 0, -0.01]) 
                    cylinder(h=base_pocket_h + 0.01, d1=d_bottom, d2=d_at_base_top);

                d_barb_top = d_bottom + (z_end / pocket_depth) * taper_range;

Before wrapping the pipe, we need to diagnose exactly what kind of leak we are fighting, because the solution is completely different depending on where the water is escaping.

1. The "Sweating" Leak (Through the Plastic Walls)

If the water is slowly beading up and weeping directly through the solid plastic of your printed Y-junction, no amount of tape on the pipe will stop it. The water is under pressure, finding the microscopic gaps between your FDM layer lines, and traveling right through the walls of the fitting.

  • The Fix: This is where that clear nail polish (nitrocellulose lacquer) trick we talked about earlier is mandatory. You have to paint the outside of the print to fuse those layer lines into a solid, impenetrable shell.

2. The Connection Leak (Around the Pipe Entry)

If the water is spraying or dripping specifically out of the gap where your physical pipe pushes into the printed Y-junction, then the issue is a micro-gap between the tube and the 3D printed barbs.

If this is the case, your instinct to wrap the pipe is exactly right, but electrical tape will likely fail you here. The adhesive turns into a slippery, gummy mess when constantly exposed to pressurized water, and the vinyl backing doesn't compress well enough to fill the microscopic gaps around the rigid plastic barbs.

Here is how the pros tackle connection leaks:

  • Teflon Tape (Plumber's PTFE Tape): This is the ultimate material for this exact problem. It has no adhesive, it's incredibly thin, and it stretches and crushes perfectly. If you wrap the end of your pipe tightly with a few layers of Teflon tape before shoving it into the Y-junction, the tape will mash into the printed layer lines and create a flawless, watertight gasket.
  • External Zip-Ties: Sometimes the simplest solution is best. Push the pipe into the fitting, and then crank a tiny zip-tie as tightly as possible around the outside of the rubber pipe, right where it sits over the printed internal barbs. This clamps the soft tube down into the rigid plastic valleys.
  • O-Rings: Rolling a tiny, tight-fitting rubber O-ring onto the tip of your pipe before inserting it will force a mechanical seal against the funnel entrance.

Your instinct that the fitting needs to physically "sustain the water pressure" is exactly right. When the system pressurizes, the water forces the flexible pipe to expand. While internal threads sound like a great mechanical lock, they are actually a trap for 3D printed fluid systems.

Why Internal Threads Fail Under Pressure

  1. The Overhang Problem: Because the Y-junction has angled branches, the internal threads would have to print mid-air inside the tube. Gravity pulls the hot plastic down, ruining the precision of the thread.
  2. The Spiral Leak: Threads create a continuous, spiral-shaped gap from the inside of the fitting to the outside. Water under pressure will follow that spiral path like a waterslide, leaking even worse than your current push-fit design.

To beat pressure, we have to copy how high-pressure automotive and off-grid plumbing actually works.

Right now, we are designing an Outer Sleeve (the pipe goes inside the 3D print). We need to flip that and print an Inner Barb (the 3D print goes inside the pipe).

When the 3D printed stem is inside the rubber pipe, you can slip a metal worm-gear hose clamp (or a very tight, thick zip-tie) over the outside of the rubber. // The 3D print goes INSIDE the tubes, allowing for external metal hose clamps.

// --- Physical Tube Inner Diameters ---
large_tube_id = 5.5; 
small_tube_id = 3.5;

large_barb_od = large_tube_id + 1.5; 
small_barb_od = small_tube_id + 1.2;

large_fluid_path = large_tube_id - 1.5;
small_fluid_path = small_tube_id - 1.0;

stem_length = 18;
barb_spacing = 4;
barb_height = 0.8;

module barbed_stem(od, id, length) {
    difference() {
        union() {
            // Base cylinder
            cylinder(h=length, d=od - (barb_height*2));
            
            // Repeating pressure barbs
            num_barbs = floor(length / barb_spacing);
            for (i = [0 : num_barbs - 1]) {
                translate([0, 0, i * barb_spacing])

        // Hollow fluid path
        translate([0, 0, -1])
            cylinder(h=length + 2, d=id);

}

    difference() {
        sphere(d=large_barb_od + 2);
        sphere(d=large_fluid_path); // Hollow center

        barbed_stem(od=large_barb_od, id=large_fluid_path, length=stem_length);

It solves the exact problem of "I can't get the pipe on" while simultaneously improving the high-pressure seal. By tapering the entire stem, you get two massive benefits:

  1. The Pilot Tip: The outer ends (the tips) are significantly narrower, acting as a pilot guide so you can effortlessly slip the rubber pipe over the first few barbs.
  2. The Compression Wedge: As you force the pipe further down toward the center hub (the inner ends), the diameter smoothly and steadily increases. This acts like a wedge, aggressively expanding the rubber. By the time you crank your metal hose clamp down over that thickest base section, the tension will be absolute.

I have updated the OpenSCAD script to calculate a progressive global taper. The stems now shrink by 1.0mm as they travel outward, while keeping the sharp 0.8mm drops on every single barb.

Copy this exact block to your clipboard:

// Tapered High-Pressure Inner Barb Y-Junction
// Features: Progressive global taper (narrow tips for insertion, wide bases for clamping)

$fn = 100;

// --- Physical Tube Inner Diameters ---
large_tube_id = 5.5; 
small_tube_id = 3.5;

// --- Base Barb Dimensions (Maximum stretch at the inner base) ---
large_barb_base_od = large_tube_id + 1.5; 
small_barb_base_od = small_tube_id + 1.2;

// --- Stem Taper (How much the diameter shrinks at the outer tips) ---
stem_taper = 1.0; // The tips will be 1.0mm smaller in diameter than the base

// --- Internal Fluid Channels ---
large_fluid_path = large_tube_id - 1.5;
small_fluid_path = small_tube_id - 1.0;

stem_length = 18;
barb_spacing = 4;
barb_height = 0.8;

module barbed_stem(od_base, id, length) {
    difference() {
        union() {
            // Repeating pressure barbs with a global taper
            num_barbs = floor(length / barb_spacing);
            for (i = [0 : num_barbs - 1]) {
                z_bottom = i * barb_spacing;
                z_top = z_bottom + barb_spacing;
                
                // Calculate the shrinking diameter as we move outward toward the tip
                local_od_bottom = od_base - (z_bottom / length) * stem_taper;
                local_od_top = od_base - (z_top / length) * stem_taper;
                
                translate([0, 0, z_bottom])
                    cylinder(h=barb_spacing, 
                             d1=local_od_bottom, 
                             d2=local_od_top - (barb_height * 2));
            }
        }
        // Hollow fluid path
        translate([0, 0, -1])
            cylinder(h=length + 2, d=id);
    }
}

module inner_barb_y_junction() {
    // Central Hub
    difference() {
        sphere(d=large_barb_base_od + 2);
        sphere(d=large_fluid_path); // Hollow center
    }
    
    // Main Input
    rotate([0, 90, 0]) 
        barbed_stem(od_base=large_barb_base_od, id=large_fluid_path, length=stem_length);
        
    // Large Output Wing (20 degrees)
    rotate([0, -90, 20]) 
        barbed_stem(od_base=large_barb_base_od, id=large_fluid_path, length=stem_length);
        
    // Small Output Wing (-35 degrees)
    rotate([0, -90, -35]) 
        barbed_stem(od_base=small_barb_base_od, id=small_fluid_path, length=stem_length);
}

// Render the part (Lay flat for strength)
translate([0, 0, (large_barb_base_od / 2)])
inner_barb_y_junction();
